segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came back into Capernaum some days later, word got out that he was at home.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And so many gathered that there was no longer any room, not even around the door, and he was speaking the word to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And some people came, bringing to him a paralyzed man carried by four of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And since they could not bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above where he was, and when they had dug through, they lowered the mat on which the paralyzed man was lying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Child, your sins are forgiven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, reasoning in their hearts,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they were reasoning this way within themselves, said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you reasoning these things in your hearts?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which is easier: to say to the paralyzed man, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat and walk’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I say to you, get up, pick up your mat and go home.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up, and immediately picked up the mat and went out in front of everyone, so that they were all astonished and glorified God, saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “We have never seen anything like this!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd kept coming to him, and he taught them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as he passed by, he saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it happened that he was reclining at table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many of them, and they were following him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the scribes of the Pharisees, seeing that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And hearing this, Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The healthy have no need of a doctor, but the sick do. I did not come to call the just, but sinners.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast, on that day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment; otherwise the patch pulls away from it, the new from the old, and the tear becomes worse.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wine will burst the skins, and the wine is lost, and the skins too. No—new wine into fresh wineskins.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it happened that he was passing through the grainfields on the Sabbath, and his disciples began to make their way, plucking the heads of grain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the Pharisees said to him,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Look, why are they doing on the Sabbath what is not permitted?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he and those with him—

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: how he went into the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the loaves of presentation, which no one is permitted to eat except the priests, and gave some also to those who were with him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The Sabbath was made for people, and not people for the Sabbath;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

notes.note: Village houses in Galilee typically had flat roofs of wooden beams overlaid with branches or reeds and packed clay, reached by an outside stair or ladder. Opening such a roof meant literally digging through it, which is the verb Mark uses.

Most English versions have ‘Son’. The Greek word is the ordinary word for ‘child’, used here as an affectionate address to an adult; it is not the word for ‘son’ that appears in ‘Son of Man’ in verse 10, and the rendering keeps the two distinct.

The Greek is literally ‘except one, God’. The wording probably echoes Israel’s daily confession that God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4), which sharpens the charge: Jesus is claiming what belongs to the one God.

This is the first occurrence in Mark of the phrase Jesus uses for himself. Behind it lies a Semitic idiom meaning ‘a human being’, and many scholars also hear an allusion to the human-like figure who is given authority in Daniel 7:13–14. How much of each sense a first hearer would have caught is disputed.

The ‘tax collectors’ of the Gospels were mostly collectors of tolls and customs duties on goods in transit, working under contract and profiting from what they took in. Capernaum lay near a border and on a trade route, so a customs post there is plausible. Such men were widely regarded as dishonest and were shunned by the observant, which explains the pairing ‘tax collectors and sinners’ in the next verses.

The Greek does not say whose house this is. Most interpreters take it as Levi’s, as Luke 5:29 states outright; some take it as Jesus’s own home in Capernaum (compare verse 1). The translation leaves the pronoun as open as the Greek.

Many later manuscripts read ‘the scribes and the Pharisees’, a more familiar phrase. The unusual wording translated here, meaning scribes who belonged to the Pharisaic party, is found in early witnesses and is generally judged original.

English divides a single Greek word-family between ‘just/justice’ and ‘righteous/righteousness’; this translation uses the ‘just’ family throughout so that the connection remains audible. Most versions prefer ‘righteous’ because the word often means being in right standing before God, which modern ‘just’ can narrow, and both choices lose something. Here it means people who are in the right with God, in contrast to ‘sinners’.

The Greek is literally ‘the sons of the wedding hall’ (or ‘bridal chamber’), a Semitic idiom for those who belong to the wedding party. It may mean the guests in general or, more narrowly, the bridegroom’s attendants. A wedding was a time of feasting, at which fasting would have been out of place.

notes.phrase: in the time of Abiathar the high priest
notes.note: In the account in 1 Samuel 21:1–6 the priest David meets is Ahimelech, the father of Abiathar; Abiathar became the better-known priest of David’s reign. Some explain the phrase as a loose dating by the more famous figure, others as meaning ‘in the passage about Abiathar’ (compare the similar expression at Mark 12:26). The difficulty is real, and no explanation is agreed; Matthew and Luke do not have the phrase.

notes.traditional: the bread of the Presence (older: the shewbread)
notes.note: The traditional ‘bread of the Presence’ translates the Hebrew expression behind the phrase. The Greek term, taken over from the Septuagint, means ‘setting out’ or ‘presentation’. It refers to the twelve loaves set out before God in the sanctuary each Sabbath, which the priests alone ate afterwards (Leviticus 24:5–9).

The traditional ‘the Sabbath was made for man’ uses ‘man’ for humanity in general, which is what the Greek word means here. The cost of ‘people’ is that English no longer shows the verbal link with ‘Son of Man’ in the next verse, where the same Greek word appears. Some scholars think the underlying saying meant that human beings are lord of the Sabbath, but Mark clearly applies the title to Jesus.
